did_you_know.text: The title presents the psalm as a song of the sons of Korah and attributes it to Heman the Ezrahite. It also describes it as a “maskil”—a psalm intended for instruction or meditation.
The psalmist addresses the LORD as “the God of my salvation,” even though he is in distress. He describes a cry that is not limited to the daytime: “I cry out by day and at night.”
The prayer is described as needing to reach the LORD, and the psalmist asks, “Incline your ear.” This emphasizes the plea for divine attentiveness alongside the act of prayer itself.

The psalmist describes his condition as being near death: his soul is full of troubles, and his life has reached the grave. The use of the words “my soul” and “my life” emphasizes that the distress encompasses his entire existence.

The speaker presents himself as someone who has lost his strength: “I am like a man without strength.” This image is paired with his description of himself as one who has descended into the pit and is counted among the dead.
The distress is described as a descent into a low, dark, and deep place: “the lowest pit,” “dark places,” and “the depths.” This sequence of images creates a picture of sinking and isolation.

Despite his weakness, the psalmist does not stop praying: he calls to the LORD every day and stretches out his hands to him. His persistence in prayer is especially striking against the backdrop of suffering and loneliness.

The psalmist asks a series of questions about death: Can the dead experience wonders, or rise to praise the LORD? These are rhetorical questions arising from his distress, highlighting his desire for deliverance while he is still alive.
The prayer does not end after a difficult night: “In the morning, my prayer comes before you.” This creates a continuing pattern of prayer at night, during the day, and in the morning.
The psalm ends without an explicit description of resolution or comfort; its final line emphasizes the departure of loved one, friend, and acquaintance, and ends with the word “darkness.”
